library(nlmixr2lib)

# Model and source

* Citation: Andersson R, Kroon T, Almquist J, Jirstrand M, Oakes ND, Evans ND,
  Chappell MJ, Gabrielsson J. Modeling of free fatty acid dynamics: insulin
  and nicotinic acid resistance under acute and chronic treatments.
  *J Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn* 2017;44(3):203-222.
* Article (open access): <https://doi.org/10.1007/s10928-017-9512-6>

The paper fits the same nicotinic acid (NiAc) - insulin - free fatty acid (FFA)
model separately to lean Sprague-Dawley and obese Zucker (fa/fa) rats, so it is
packaged as two models:

* `Andersson_2017_nicotinicAcid_lean_rat`: two-compartment NiAc disposition
  with two Michaelis-Menten pathways; fixed NiAc efficacy on insulin; dynamic
  (down-regulated) NiAc efficacy on FFA.
* `Andersson_2017_nicotinicAcid_obese_rat`: one-compartment NiAc disposition
  with one Michaelis-Menten pathway; dynamic NiAc efficacy on both insulin and
  FFA.

Both models use the same structure for insulin and FFA turnover. NiAc inhibits
production (an Imax-Hill function). A moderator feedback acts on production
(and, for insulin, a second moderator acts on loss). An insulin-driven integral
controller, the regulator, acts on production; its set point is the baseline
insulin I0.

```{r load-models}
mod_lean <- readModelDb("Andersson_2017_nicotinicAcid_lean_rat")
mod_obese <- readModelDb("Andersson_2017_nicotinicAcid_obese_rat")
ui_lean <- rxode2::rxode2(mod_lean)
ui_obese <- rxode2::rxode2(mod_obese)
typ_lean <- rxode2::zeroRe(ui_lean)
typ_obese <- rxode2::zeroRe(ui_obese)
```

# Population

Male lean Sprague-Dawley rats and obese Zucker (fa/fa) rats were studied at
AstraZeneca, Gothenburg (Table 1 of the paper). There were seven protocols:

* three conscious protocols with s.c. infusion from an implanted programmable
  mini-pump: acute 5 h (NiAc naive), 5 h after 5 days of continuous infusion
  (Cont. NiAc), and 5 h after 5 days of 12 h on / 12 h off infusion
  (Inter. NiAc);
* two anesthetized protocols with 1 h of i.v. infusion, followed by an
  abrupt stop (Off 1 h) or a 3.5 h step-down (Stp-Dwn 1 h);
* two anesthetized protocols with 12 h of s.c. infusion, followed by an
  abrupt stop (Off 12 h) or a step-down (Stp-Dwn 12 h).

The nominal rate was 170 nmol/min/kg (10.2 umol/kg/h). Table 1 lists 38 lean
and 41 obese rats; saline-infused controls are given in parentheses there.
Age and body weight were not reported. All parameters are per kg of body
weight.

```{r population}
str(ui_lean$population[c("species", "n_subjects", "n_studies")])
str(ui_obese$population[c("species", "n_subjects", "n_studies")])
```

# Source trace

Every `ini()` value carries an in-file comment that points to its source.
Equations are from the Methods and Appendix 2 of the paper.

| Equation / parameter | Lean | Obese | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| NiAc disposition | 2-cmt, 2 MM pathways | 1-cmt, 1 MM pathway | Eqs. 1-2 (lean), Eq. 6 (obese) |
| s.c. pump input `Pump rate = Inf.rate * erf(t delta / sqrt(t0))` | yes | yes | Eqs. 3-5, Appendix 1 |
| Endogenous NiAc baseline | positive quadratic root | `Synt*Km1/(Vmax1-Synt)` | Appendix 2, Eqs. 33-37 |
| Insulin turnover, moderators, regulator | Eqs. 7-14 | Eqs. 7-14 | Methods |
| NiAc inhibition of insulin, `E_NI` | fixed `ImaxNI` | dynamic (Eqs. 16-17) | Eqs. 15-17 |
| FFA turnover, moderator, regulator, dynamic efficacy | Eqs. 20-27 | Eqs. 20-27 | Methods |
| `kinI = koutI*I0`, `kinF = koutF*F0`, `kinR = koutR*I0` | yes | yes | Appendix 2 Eqs. 39, 41; Eqs. 13, 24 |
| `ka` (1/h) | 4.27 | 5.54 | Table 2 |
| `delta` | 77.4 | 62.4 | Table 2 |
| `Vmax1` (umol/kg/h) | 2.64 | 164 | Table 2 |
| `Km1` (umol/L) | 0.235 (fixed) | 18.9 (fixed) | Table 2, from Tapani et al. |
| `Vmax2`, `Km2` | 425, 74.5 (fixed) | n/a | Table 2, from Tapani et al. |
| `Vp`, `Vt` (L/kg) | 0.393, 0.172 (fixed) | 0.323 (fixed) | Table 2, from Tapani et al. |
| `Cld` (L/kg/h) | 0.0511 (fixed) | n/a | Table 2, from Tapani et al. |
| `Synt` (umol/kg/h) | 0.213 (fixed) | 0.168 (fixed) | Table 2, from Tapani et al. |
| `I0` (nM), `koutI` (1/h) | 0.188, 6.58 | 3.26, 10.8 | Table 2 |
| `ImaxNI`, `IC50NI` (uM), `n` | 0.793, 0.338, 3.54 | 1 (fixed), 0.175, 0.840 | Table 2 |
| `ktolI` (1/h), `koutRI` (1/nM/h) | 0.646, 3.94 | 0.125, 0.0612 | Table 2 |
| `kNI`, `N50I`, `gamma`, `SNI` | n/a | 0.0242, 0.897, 18.9, 1 (fixed) | Table 2 |
| `F0` (mM), `koutF` (1/h) | 0.707, 428 | 1.14, 173 | Table 2 |
| `ImaxNF`, `IC50NF` (uM), `m` | 1 (fixed), 0.436, 1.24 | 1 (fixed), 0.456, 0.731 | Table 2 |
| `ktolF` (1/h), `koutRF` (1/nM/h) | 1.21, 0.965 | 0.708, 0.0165 | Table 2 |
| `kNF`, `N50F`, `phi`, `SNF` | 0.00654, 3.05, 1 (fixed), 0.807 | 0.0377, 0.854, 8.83, 1 (fixed) | Table 2 |
| BSV (CV%, `omega^2 = (CV/100)^2`) | Table 2 | Table 2 | Table 2 footnote a |
| Residual error | prop. 0.313; add. 0.0699 nM; add. 0.130 mM | prop. 0.483; add. 0.748 nM; add. 0.135 mM | Table 2 |

# Protocols

The helper below writes a NiAc infusion schedule as dose rows. s.c. doses go to
the `pump` compartment and i.v. doses go to `central`. A schedule is a table of
infusion segments with a start time, a duration and a rate (umol/kg/h).

```{r protocols}
rate_nom <- 170 * 60 / 1000 # 170 nmol/min/kg = 10.2 umol/kg/h

# Step-down rates (nmol/min/kg), 0.5 h each (Methods)
step_12h <- c(88.9, 58.3, 43.7, 34.0, 24.3, 17.0, 9.7) * 60 / 1000
step_1h <- c(31.1, 20.4, 15.3, 11.9, 8.50, 5.95, 3.40) * 60 / 1000

protocols <- list(
  "Naive" = list(cmt = "pump", start = 1, dur = 5, rate = rate_nom, from = 0, to = 10),
  "Inter." = list(
    cmt = "pump", start = c(0, 24, 48, 72, 96, 120),
    dur = c(12, 12, 12, 12, 12, 5), rate = rate_nom, from = 118, to = 128
  ),
  "Cont." = list(cmt = "pump", start = 0, dur = 125, rate = rate_nom, from = 118, to = 128),
  "Off 12h" = list(cmt = "pump", start = 0, dur = 12, rate = rate_nom, from = 10, to = 18),
  "Stp-Dwn 12h" = list(
    cmt = "pump", start = c(0, 12 + 0.5 * (0:6)), dur = c(12, rep(0.5, 7)),
    rate = c(rate_nom, step_12h), from = 10, to = 18
  ),
  "Off 1h" = list(cmt = "central", start = 0.5, dur = 1, rate = rate_nom, from = 0, to = 6.5),
  "Stp-Dwn 1h" = list(
    cmt = "central", start = c(0.5, 1.5 + 0.5 * (0:6)), dur = c(1, rep(0.5, 7)),
    rate = c(rate_nom, step_1h), from = 0, to = 6.5
  )
)

dose_rows <- function(p) {
  data.frame(
    time = p$start, amt = p$rate * p$dur, rate = p$rate,
    cmt = p$cmt, evid = 1L, dvid = NA_integer_, ep = NA_integer_
  )
}

# Observation rows on the ODE states (dvid 1 = NiAc Cc on central,
# 2 = insulin, 3 = FFA); rxode2 returns every algebraic output on each row.
# `ep` repeats the endpoint number so it can ride through rxSolve via `keep`.
obs_rows <- function(times) {
  data.frame(
    time = rep(times, 3), amt = NA_real_, rate = NA_real_,
    cmt = rep(c("central", "insulin", "nefa"), each = length(times)),
    evid = 0L, dvid = rep(1:3, each = length(times)),
    ep = rep(1:3, each = length(times))
  )
}

protocol_events <- function(p, by = 0.02) {
  times <- sort(unique(c(seq(p$from, p$to, by = by), p$start, p$start + p$dur)))
  times <- times[times >= p$from & times <= p$to]
  ev <- rbind(dose_rows(p), obs_rows(times))
  ev[order(ev$time, -ev$evid), ]
}

solve_typical <- function(mod, ev) {
  as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(mod, ev,
    keep = "ep", useLinCmt = FALSE,
    atol = 1e-10, rtol = 1e-10
  ))
}
```

# Typical-value replication of Figures 7 and 8

Figures 7 (lean) and 8 (obese) show visual predictive checks: the median
individual and a 90% prediction interval for every protocol. The paper's
medians include fixed study effects on the insulin and FFA baselines and on the
moderator rates. Only their weighted summaries (the Table 2 estimates) are
printed, so the typical-value curves below reproduce the shapes but not the
exact per-protocol baselines.

```{r typical-sims}
typ_all <- lapply(names(protocols), function(nm) {
  p <- protocols[[nm]]
  ev <- protocol_events(p)
  rbind(
    solve_typical(typ_lean, ev) |> filter(ep == 1) |>
      transmute(protocol = nm, strain = "lean", time, Cc, insulin, nefa),
    solve_typical(typ_obese, ev) |> filter(ep == 1) |>
      transmute(protocol = nm, strain = "obese", time, Cc, insulin, nefa)
  )
}) |> bind_rows()
typ_all$protocol <- factor(typ_all$protocol, levels = names(protocols))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(typ_all$Cc)), all(is.finite(typ_all$nefa)))
```

```{r fig7-8-pk, fig.height = 7}
ggplot(typ_all, aes(time, Cc, colour = strain)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~protocol, scales = "free_x", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "NiAc (umol/L)", colour = NULL,
       caption = "Typical-value NiAc; replicates the first column of Figures 7 and 8.")
```

```{r fig7-8-insulin, fig.height = 7}
ggplot(typ_all, aes(time, insulin, colour = strain)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~protocol, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "Insulin (nmol/L)", colour = NULL,
       caption = "Typical-value insulin; replicates the second column of Figures 7 and 8.")
```

```{r fig7-8-ffa, fig.height = 7}
ggplot(typ_all, aes(time, nefa, colour = strain)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~protocol, scales = "free_x", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "FFA (mmol/L)", colour = NULL,
       caption = "Typical-value FFA; replicates the third column of Figures 7 and 8.")
```

# Validation against the paper

## NiAc exposure: Figures 7a and 8a

Figures 7a and 8a are vector graphics in the article PDF. The maintainers
extracted the median-individual curves for the NiAc naive protocol (s.c. pump
on from 1 to 6 h) from the drawing coordinates, using the plot's own tick marks
for calibration. The PK median carries no study effect, so a deterministic
typical-value solve should match it.

```{r pk-digitized}
fig_pk <- tibble::tribble(
  ~strain, ~time, ~Cc_fig,
  "lean",  0.50, 0.01304,
  "lean",  1.44, 0.187,
  "lean",  1.73, 0.4116,
  "lean",  1.97, 0.7225,
  "lean",  2.27, 1.004,
  "lean",  2.695, 1.19,
  "lean",  5.00, 1.447,
  "obese", 0.50, 0.0194,
  "obese", 1.30, 0.131,
  "obese", 1.635, 0.364,
  "obese", 2.318, 0.887,
  "obese", 2.747, 1.03,
  "obese", 5.00, 1.276
)

pk_check <- function(tidle) {
  p <- protocols[["Naive"]]
  ev <- rbind(dose_rows(p), obs_rows(unique(fig_pk$time)))
  ev <- ev[order(ev$time, -ev$evid), ]
  prm <- c(tidle_pump = tidle)
  bind_rows(
    as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(typ_lean, ev, params = prm, keep = "ep", useLinCmt = FALSE)) |>
      filter(ep == 1) |> transmute(strain = "lean", time, Cc),
    as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(typ_obese, ev, params = prm, keep = "ep", useLinCmt = FALSE)) |>
      filter(ep == 1) |> transmute(strain = "obese", time, Cc)
  ) |>
    inner_join(fig_pk, by = c("strain", "time")) |>
    mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (Cc - Cc_fig) / Cc_fig)
}

pk_min <- pk_check(10080)
pk_hour <- pk_check(168)

pk_min |>
  left_join(pk_hour |> select(strain, time, Cc_t0_168h = Cc), by = c("strain", "time")) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 3))) |>
  rename(
    "Strain" = strain, "Time (h)" = time,
    "Model, t0 = 10080 min" = Cc, "Figure median" = Cc_fig,
    "% difference" = pct_diff, "Model, t0 = 168 h" = Cc_t0_168h
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "NiAc (umol/L): typical-value solve vs the Figure 7a / 8a median.")

# Baseline (endogenous NiAc) and plateau are set by Synt, Vmax and Km alone.
base_plat <- pk_min |> filter(time %in% c(0.5, 5))
stopifnot(all(abs(base_plat$pct_diff) < 3))
# The rising limb is set by ka and the pump erf term.
stopifnot(all(abs(pk_min$pct_diff) < 20))
# Reading t0 = 7 days as 168 h makes the erf term negligible and the rise far
# too fast, which the figure rules out.
stopifnot(pk_hour$Cc[pk_hour$strain == "lean" & pk_hour$time == 1.44] > 3 * 0.187)
```

The endogenous baselines (0.0130 and 0.0194 umol/L) and the plateaus (1.45 and
1.28 umol/L) agree with the figure within 3%. The text says the plateau is
"about 1 umol/L". The rising limb fixes how the pump time in Eq. 5 is read. The
text gives the pump inactivation time t0 as "7 days". Entered as 168 h, the
erf term reaches 1 within minutes, and NiAc at 0.44 h after pump start is
about 5 times the figure value. Entered as 10080 min (with t still in hours),
the model reproduces the roughly 1.5 h dilution period that the Results
describe ("the NiAc dosing solution was diluted during the first ~1.5 h"). The
packaged models therefore use `tidle_pump = 10080`.

## Model simulations of NiAc, insulin and moderator action: Figure 9

Figure 9 shows typical-value simulations of a long NiAc infusion in lean and
obese rats, which ends at 125 h. The plotted quantities are:

* NiAc action on FFA turnover, `H_NF`;
* insulin action, the FFA regulator `R_F`;
* moderator action, `F0/M_F`;
* the FFA response.

It was also extracted from the vector PDF. The simulation below uses the
nominal s.c. pump rate from t = 0 to 125 h.

```{r fig9}
ev9 <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    time = 0, amt = rate_nom * 125, rate = rate_nom, cmt = "pump",
    evid = 1L, dvid = NA_integer_, ep = NA_integer_
  ),
  obs_rows(sort(unique(c(seq(0, 12, by = 0.02), 2.21, 2.45, 4.41, seq(118, 128, by = 0.02)))))
)
ev9 <- ev9[order(ev9$time, -ev9$evid), ]
fig9_sim <- bind_rows(
  solve_typical(typ_lean, ev9) |> filter(ep == 3) |> mutate(strain = "lean"),
  solve_typical(typ_obese, ev9) |> filter(ep == 3) |> mutate(strain = "obese")
) |>
  transmute(strain, time,
    `NiAc action (%)` = 100 * inh_nefa,
    `Insulin action (%)` = 100 * regulator_nefa,
    `Moderator action (%)` = 100 * rbase_nefa / moderator3,
    `FFA (mM)` = nefa
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(strain, time), names_to = "quantity")

# Values read from Figure 9 (time 0, early infusion, and the chronic state at
# 118-124 h, before the infusion stops at 125 h).
fig9_dig <- tibble::tribble(
  ~strain, ~quantity, ~time, ~fig,
  "lean",  "NiAc action (%)", 0, 98.77,
  "obese", "NiAc action (%)", 0, 90.06,
  "lean",  "NiAc action (%)", 12, 20.53,
  "obese", "NiAc action (%)", 12, 30.66,
  "lean",  "NiAc action (%)", 120, 31.81,
  "obese", "NiAc action (%)", 120, 97.9,
  "lean",  "Insulin action (%)", 12, 151.8,
  "obese", "Insulin action (%)", 12, 132.2,
  "lean",  "Insulin action (%)", 120, 190.0,
  "obese", "Insulin action (%)", 120, 104.1,
  "lean",  "Moderator action (%)", 120, 129.1,
  "obese", "Moderator action (%)", 120, 99.3,
  "lean",  "FFA (mM)", 120, 0.551,
  "obese", "FFA (mM)", 120, 1.145,
  "lean",  "Moderator action (%)", 2.45, 118.0,
  "obese", "Moderator action (%)", 4.41, 135.1,
  "lean",  "FFA (mM)", 2.2, 0.184,
  "obese", "FFA (mM)", 2.21, 0.459
)
fig9_cmp <- fig9_dig |>
  mutate(time_key = round(time, 2)) |>
  left_join(
    fig9_sim |> mutate(time_key = round(time, 2)) |> select(-time),
    by = c("strain", "quantity", "time_key")
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (value - fig) / fig)

fig9_cmp |>
  select(strain, quantity, time, fig, value, pct_diff) |>
  mutate(across(c(fig, value, pct_diff), \(x) signif(x, 3))) |>
  rename("Strain" = strain, "Quantity" = quantity, "Time (h)" = time,
         "Figure 9" = fig, "Model" = value, "% difference" = pct_diff) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Figure 9 values vs the typical-value solve.")

# Time 0: the endogenous NiAc level already inhibits FFA production
# (Appendix 2 assumes Cp(0) ~ 0); the figure shows the same offset.
chk0 <- fig9_cmp |> filter(time == 0)
stopifnot(all(abs(chk0$value - chk0$fig) < 1))
# Plateau and chronic (118-124 h) state: independent of the moderator rate.
chk_ss <- fig9_cmp |> filter(time %in% c(12, 120))
stopifnot(all(abs(chk_ss$pct_diff) < 6))
```

```{r fig9-plot, fig.height = 6}
fig9_sim |>
  mutate(phase = ifelse(time <= 12, "0-12 h", "118-128 h")) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, value, colour = strain)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = fig9_dig |> mutate(value = fig, phase = ifelse(time <= 12, "0-12 h", "118-128 h")),
             shape = 1, size = 2) +
  facet_grid(quantity ~ phase, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = NULL, colour = NULL,
       caption = "Lines: model. Circles: values read from Figure 9 of Andersson 2017.")
```

At time 0 the model and the figure agree within 1 percentage point. Both show
that the endogenous NiAc level already lowers FFA turnover by 1% (lean) and 9%
(obese). On the infusion plateau and in the chronic state at 120 h, `H_NF`,
`R_F`, the moderator action and FFA all agree within 6%. That chronic state is
where the paper's main claims sit. In lean rats, NiAc efficacy falls by about
13% and insulin action rises to about 190%. In obese rats, NiAc action and
insulin action return to baseline. The rebound after the infusion stops at
125 h also appears in lean rats and not in obese rats.

The acute moderator response does not match. In Figure 9 the moderator action
rises several-fold more slowly than Table 2's `ktolF` allows (1.21 and
0.708 1/h, half-lives of 0.57 and 0.98 h, which Table 3 repeats). Because of
this, the FFA nadir in the figure is deeper: 0.18 vs 0.32 mM in lean rats, and
0.46 vs 0.62 mM in obese rats. The figure behaves as if `ktolF` were about
one-sixth of the Table 2 value in both strains. The NiAc naive VPC median in
Figure 7c also reaches about 0.18 mM. The packaged models keep the Table 2
estimates, which Table 3 confirms independently, and record the discrepancy
here. They are not tuned to the figure.

## Turnover half-lives: Table 3

Table 3 lists `log(2)/k` for each turnover process. Recomputing it from the
packaged parameters checks the transcription of every rate constant.

```{r table3}
hl <- function(ui, nm) log(2) / exp(ui$theta[[nm]])
t3 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~process, ~analyte, ~strain, ~paper, ~model,
  "Biomarker", "Insulin", "lean", 0.105, hl(ui_lean, "lkout_insulin"),
  "Biomarker", "FFA", "lean", 0.00162, hl(ui_lean, "lkout_nefa"),
  "Biomarker", "Insulin", "obese", 0.0643, hl(ui_obese, "lkout_insulin"),
  "Biomarker", "FFA", "obese", 0.00401, hl(ui_obese, "lkout_nefa"),
  "Moderator", "Insulin", "lean", 1.07, hl(ui_lean, "lktol_insulin"),
  "Moderator", "FFA", "lean", 0.570, hl(ui_lean, "lktol_nefa"),
  "Moderator", "Insulin", "obese", 5.53, hl(ui_obese, "lktol_insulin"),
  "Moderator", "FFA", "obese", 0.979, hl(ui_obese, "lktol_nefa"),
  "Controller", "Insulin", "lean", 0.176, hl(ui_lean, "lkoutr_insulin"),
  "Controller", "FFA", "lean", 0.719, hl(ui_lean, "lkoutr_nefa"),
  "Controller", "Insulin", "obese", 11.3, hl(ui_obese, "lkoutr_insulin"),
  "Controller", "FFA", "obese", 42.0, hl(ui_obese, "lkoutr_nefa"),
  "NiAc action", "FFA", "lean", 106, hl(ui_lean, "lkn_nefa"),
  "NiAc action", "Insulin", "obese", 28.7, hl(ui_obese, "lkn_insulin"),
  "NiAc action", "FFA", "obese", 18.4, hl(ui_obese, "lkn_nefa")
) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (model - paper) / paper)
t3 |>
  mutate(across(c(model, pct_diff), \(x) signif(x, 3))) |>
  rename("Process" = process, "Analyte" = analyte, "Strain" = strain,
         "Table 3 (h)" = paper, "Model (h)" = model, "% difference" = pct_diff) |>
  knitr::kable()
# Rounding of the printed rate constants only (0.125 1/h gives 5.55 h, not 5.53)
stopifnot(all(abs(t3$pct_diff) < 1))
```

The controller half-life in Table 3 is `log(2)/koutR`. It treats the integral
gain (1/nM/h) as a rate constant.

The Results also give absorption half-lives of 0.16 and 0.13 h:

```{r absorption-halflife}
ka_hl <- c(lean = log(2) / exp(ui_lean$theta[["lka"]]), obese = log(2) / exp(ui_obese$theta[["lka"]]))
signif(ka_hl, 3)
stopifnot(abs(ka_hl[["lean"]] - 0.16) < 0.005, abs(ka_hl[["obese"]] - 0.13) < 0.005)
```

## NCA of the 1 h i.v. infusion (PKNCA)

During the 1 h i.v. infusion, plasma NiAc approaches steady state within
minutes. That steady state has a closed form (Appendix 2, Eqs. 33-37) with
`alpha = Inf.rate + Synt`. For the lean rat it is the positive root of a
quadratic. For the obese rat it is `alpha*Km1/(Vmax1 - alpha)`. PKNCA's
`cmax` for the typical-value profile should match it within 1%. The small
lean shortfall is the tissue compartment, which is still filling
(`Vt/Cld` = 3.4 h).

```{r pknca}
p_iv <- protocols[["Off 1h"]]
ev_iv <- rbind(dose_rows(p_iv), obs_rows(c(0, seq(0.5, 6.5, by = 0.01))))
ev_iv <- ev_iv[order(ev_iv$time, -ev_iv$evid), ]
conc_iv <- bind_rows(
  solve_typical(typ_lean, ev_iv) |> filter(ep == 1) |> mutate(id = 1L, treatment = "lean"),
  solve_typical(typ_obese, ev_iv) |> filter(ep == 1) |> mutate(id = 2L, treatment = "obese")
) |>
  select(id, treatment, time, Cc) |>
  filter(!is.na(Cc))
dose_iv <- data.frame(id = 1:2, treatment = c("lean", "obese"), time = 0.5, amt = rate_nom * 1)

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc_iv, Cc ~ time | treatment + id)
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_iv, amt ~ time | treatment + id)
intervals <- data.frame(start = 0.5, end = 6.5, cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE, auclast = TRUE)
nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals))
nca_tab <- as.data.frame(nca_res$result) |>
  select(treatment, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = PPORRES)

th_lean <- exp(ui_lean$theta)
alpha_lean <- rate_nom + th_lean[["lsynt"]]
qa <- alpha_lean - th_lean[["lvmax"]] - th_lean[["lvmax2"]]
qb <- alpha_lean * (th_lean[["lkm"]] + th_lean[["lkm2"]]) -
  th_lean[["lvmax"]] * th_lean[["lkm2"]] - th_lean[["lvmax2"]] * th_lean[["lkm"]]
qc <- alpha_lean * th_lean[["lkm"]] * th_lean[["lkm2"]]
css_lean <- (-qb - sqrt(qb^2 - 4 * qa * qc)) / (2 * qa)

th_obese <- exp(ui_obese$theta)
alpha_obese <- rate_nom + th_obese[["lsynt"]]
css_obese <- alpha_obese * th_obese[["lkm"]] / (th_obese[["lvmax"]] - alpha_obese)
nca_tab$css_closed_form <- c(css_lean, css_obese)
nca_tab |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 4))) |>
  rename("Strain" = treatment, "Cmax (umol/L)" = cmax, "Tmax (h)" = tmax,
         "AUClast (h*umol/L)" = auclast, "Closed-form Css (umol/L)" = css_closed_form) |>
  knitr::kable()
stopifnot(all(abs(nca_tab$cmax / nca_tab$css_closed_form - 1) < 0.01))
```

The paper reports no NCA. The Results do state the steady-state NiAc
elimination rate ("~20 and ~25 umol/kg/h for lean and obese rats"). At steady
state, elimination equals input, which is 10.2 umol/kg/h plus `Synt`. The
stated values are about twice that, so they cannot be reproduced from the
stated infusion rate and are not used as a check.

# Stochastic simulation (NiAc naive protocol)

The chunk below simulates 100 rats per strain on the NiAc naive protocol with
between-subject variability and residual error. The obese model has very wide
BSV on the insulin moderator rate (310% CV) and on `IC50NI` (190% CV), so its
insulin interval is wide. The paper's figures show the same.

```{r vpc}
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20170301)
n_per <- 100
p_naive <- protocols[["Naive"]]
ev_one <- protocol_events(p_naive, by = 0.1)
ev_vpc <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(n_per), function(i) mutate(ev_one, id = i)))
vpc <- bind_rows(
  as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(ui_lean, ev_vpc, keep = "ep", useLinCmt = FALSE)) |>
    mutate(strain = "lean"),
  as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(ui_obese, ev_vpc, keep = "ep", useLinCmt = FALSE)) |>
    mutate(strain = "obese")
)
endpoint_name <- c("NiAc (umol/L)", "Insulin (nmol/L)", "FFA (mmol/L)")
vpc_sum <- vpc |>
  filter(!is.na(ep)) |>
  mutate(endpoint = endpoint_name[ep]) |>
  group_by(strain, endpoint, time) |>
  summarise(
    p05 = quantile(sim, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
    p50 = median(sim, na.rm = TRUE),
    p95 = quantile(sim, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
ggplot(vpc_sum, aes(time, p50, colour = strain, fill = strain)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = p05, ymax = p95), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~endpoint, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = NULL, colour = NULL, fill = NULL,
       caption = "Median and 90% interval, 100 rats per strain; compare with Figures 7a-c and 8a-c.")

# Pre-dose FFA medians sit near F0 (BSV 17.8% lean, 0.9% obese plus the
# additive residual error); a mis-scaled F0 moves these by far more than 20%.
pre_ffa <- vpc_sum |> filter(endpoint == "FFA (mmol/L)", time == 0)
stopifnot(abs(pre_ffa$p50[pre_ffa$strain == "lean"] / 0.707 - 1) < 0.2)
stopifnot(abs(pre_ffa$p50[pre_ffa$strain == "obese"] / 1.14 - 1) < 0.2)
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Pump inactivation time t0.** Eq. 5 gives `t0` as "7 days", with no unit
  for the formula. Only `t0 = 10080` (7 days in minutes) with `t` in hours
  reproduces the rising limb of Figures 7a and 8a and the stated 1.5 h dilution
  period, so the models use `tidle_pump = fixed(10080)`. Table 2 prints the
  unit of `delta` as h^(1/2), and the Results as h^(-1/2). Under the reading
  used here, `delta` is simply the estimated constant in
  `erf(t[h] * delta / sqrt(10080))`.
* **Pump compartment.** rxode2 cannot multiply an infusion rate by a
  time-varying factor. So the programmed s.c. rate is dosed into a `pump`
  compartment that empties into the s.c. depot with a fixed rate constant of
  1000 1/h, a lag of about 4 s. The transfer is scaled by the erf factor of
  Eq. 5. That rate constant is a numerical device, not a parameter of the
  paper. `t` in the erf is the time since the first dose into `pump`
  (`tafd(pump)`). This follows Appendix 1, which assumes the dilution only
  matters before the pump first starts. For i.v. infusions, dose `central`
  directly.
* **Endogenous NiAc at baseline.** Appendix 2 derives `kinI = koutI*I0` and
  `kinF = koutF*F0` assuming `Cp(0) ~ 0`. The endogenous NiAc level
  (0.013 umol/L lean, 0.019 umol/L obese) still enters `H_NI` and `H_NF`. So
  the obese insulin and FFA fall briefly at time 0 even without a dose,
  before the integral controller restores them. Figures 8b, 8c and 9 show the
  same initial dip, which confirms that the authors simulated it this way.
  The models reproduce it as published.
* **Appendix 2 typos.** Eq. 33 repeats the pathway-1 term where the
  pathway-2 term belongs, and Eq. 34 prints the root `(-b + sqrt(...))/(2a)`.
  With `a < 0 < c` that root is negative. The models use the positive root,
  `(-b - sqrt(...))/(2a)`. Eq. 40 also mentions an insulin term
  (`ImaxIF`, `IC50IF`) that is not part of the final FFA model.
* **Parameters from the literature.** Table 2 marks literature values (from
  Tapani et al.) in blue. The open-access PDF reproduces the table without
  that colour. The Methods state that only `ka`, `delta` and `Vmax1` were
  estimated among the PK parameters, so `Km1`, `Vmax2`, `Km2`, `Vp`, `Vt`,
  `Cld` and `Synt` are `fixed()`. The BSV on `Synt` was estimated.
* **BSV on obese `Synt`.** The Methods say `Synt` varied only in lean rats,
  but Table 2 prints a BSV of 95% for obese rats. The table is followed.
* **Fixed study effects.** `I0`, `ktolI`, `F0` and `ktolF` had a separate
  fixed effect per study group. Only their weighted summaries (Table 2) and
  the baseline ranges are printed: insulin 0.151-0.264 (lean) and
  2.69-4.82 nM (obese); FFA 0.652-0.801 (lean) and 0.789-1.22 mM (obese). The
  models carry the weighted summaries as typical values.
* **Text vs table.** The Results quote median insulin baselines of 0.233 and
  3.51 nM, and an FFA efficacy-loss Hill coefficient `phi` of 8.37 for obese
  rats. Table 2 gives 0.188, 3.26 and 8.83. The table values are used.
* **Figure 9 moderator kinetics.** See above: the acute FFA moderator response
  in Figure 9 (and in the VPC median of Figure 7c) is slower than Table 2's
  `ktolF` implies. The steady states agree.
* **Figures 10 and 11, steady-state predictions.** With a constant
  0.5 umol/L, the obese model's 24 h FFA lowering is largest near 0.5 umol/L,
  as the paper reports. But its magnitude is smaller than the reported
  7.40 mM h. The steady state depends on the history of the integral
  controller, and the paper does not say how it computed that state. In
  Figure 11, NiAc action at 0.5 umol/L is about 32%. Figure 9 shows the same
  32% only at the 1.3 umol/L infusion plateau. So these predictions are not
  used as checks.
* **Residual error.** NiAc is proportional. Insulin and FFA are additive.
  Each endpoint has its own `dvid` (1 = NiAc on `central`, 2 = `insulin`,
  3 = `nefa`).
